drip.author: beavertales
drip.title: September in Ottawa: the jacket comes to work with you but it doesn't actually do anything
drip.body:
Six degrees at the bus stop this morning. Twenty-four by lunch. My jacket has spent the whole week riding the bus in, hanging on the back of a chair all day, and riding the bus home again.

It's basically on secondment. Shows up every day, no actual duties, gone by spring. I respect it. It's a good jacket.

comments.author: maplebound
comments.body: The official Ottawa answer is a fleece vest, which is a jacket that has committed to nothing. I wear mine from mid-September until the first snow. It knows it isn't a real jacket and it's at peace with that.

replies.author: beavertales
replies.body: The vest is a jacket on a four-day week. Honestly it's living the dream.

comments.author: left_on_red
comments.body: toronto version: same weather, except the jacket also has to survive a subway platform that feels like a sauna year round. there is no correct layer. there's just suffering in stages

drip.author: maplebound
drip.title: Squeezed in one more evening paddle on the canal before the boating season wraps up
drip.body:
Put in at Dow's Lake after work and paddled toward downtown while the light went. The trees along Colonel By are just starting to turn, there were maybe four other boats on the water, and the whole city was doing its commute on the pathways without once looking down at us.

The canal closes to boats after Thanksgiving, then they drop the water and we all stand around waiting for it to freeze into the Skateway. I like knowing I got one more in.

comments.author: beavertales
comments.body: Did you see the canoe man? Last I checked, he and the kayaker had reached some kind of truce where they nod at each other now. Took them all summer. Diplomacy in this town moves at exactly the speed of paddling.

replies.author: maplebound
replies.body: No sign of him, but a canoe passed me at a pace I'd describe as late for a briefing. I'm choosing to believe.

comments.author: trailmixtake
comments.body: Adding 'paddle through the middle of a capital city at dusk' to the list. Not many cities let you do that without a permit and a lecture. Does it get busy on weekends, or is it mostly commuters watching from the path?

replies.author: maplebound
replies.body: Summer weekends it's a floating traffic jam of rental kayaks. September weeknights it's yours. That's the trick to most of this town, really.

drip.author: beavertales
drip.title: Cold rain Saturday, so I did a pho crawl down Somerset. No regrets and almost no puns
drip.body:
First properly grey, cold, sideways-rain day of the fall, and this city only has one sensible response: walk down Somerset through Chinatown and go into whichever pho place has the most fogged-up windows. Fogged windows mean the broth has been on since dawn. That's science. Or at least it's my science.

Had two bowls at two different spots. My wife asked if I was okay. I told her I was pho-ine. Twenty-two years and she still lets me finish the sentence, which is love.

comments.author: maplebound
comments.body: Fogged-up windows is a real metric and I've been using it for years without having the words for it. Also, two bowls is just one bowl and a second opinion. Perfectly reasonable.

comments.author: umami_bomb
comments.body: Your science holds up better than you'd think. The long simmer is what pulls gelatin out of the bones, which is where that lip-sticking body comes from, and the charred onion and ginger at the start are doing the aroma work. A place that started its broth at dawn is a place that respects the process.

replies.author: beavertales
replies.body: 'A place that respects the process' is going on a little sign over my stove. My wife will have thoughts.

late_comments.author: maplebound
late_comments.body: Came back to this one for the September sequel: everyone's back from the lake, the buses are full again, and that same patio at 12:05 now comes with a wait, a heat lamp, and a fleece vest on every chair.
